sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A proposed study involving 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau was cancelled after facing accusations of being unethical and neocolonial. The trial, funded by the US, planned to withhold a hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants. Following public outcry and government intervention, the trial was prohibited, and police seized a batch of vaccines from the Bandim Health Project research centre.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The trial sparked international criticism because it withheld a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization in a country where the infection is widespread. Experts argued that vulnerable populations were being exposed to risks that would not be accepted in wealthier nations. The controversy also highlighted tensions regarding research ethics and the influence of US vaccine policy.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Guinea-Bissau officials are considering introducing the birth-dose vaccine into the routine immunisation schedule earlier than the previously planned 2028 date. Meanwhile, police investigations into the seized vaccines and the circumstances surrounding the research centre continue.

articles.standfirst: Exclusive: Government should introduce ‘flexi-jobs’ alongside subsidies and skills support, former minister will say

gist: The Milburn review proposes state-subsidised jobs for disabled young people.
Recommendations include flexi-jobs and job carving to improve employment access.
Proposals to fund support via disability benefit cuts face potential opposition.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Milburn review of youth employment is set to recommend an opportunity revolution for disabled 16- to 24-year-olds. It proposes state-subsidised roles, including Danish-style flexi-jobs and job carving, to help those currently not in education, employment or training.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Nearly half of young people not in work are disabled or in ill health. The review warns that failing to address this risks creating a lost generation, as many face significant barriers to employment.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The review will be published this month. While it suggests funding support by reallocating disability benefit spending, this approach may face criticism from campaigners and some Labour MPs who fear it could increase poverty.

articles.title: Swapping from dairy to plant-based milk, cheese and yoghurt ‘could lead to micronutrient deficiencies’
articles.standfirst: Young people and women most at risk, study finds, as researchers call for vegan products to be fortified with iodine in particular

gist: Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives may cause vital micronutrient deficiencies.
Iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12 levels could fall without mandatory fortification.
Young women and adolescent girls are identified as the most vulnerable population groups.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study published in the Lancet Planetary Health indicates that replacing dairy products with plant-based alternatives may lead to deficiencies in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12. Researchers modelled the impact of substituting dairy with non-dairy milks, yoghurts and cheeses, noting that many current products lack sufficient fortification.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Iodine is essential for thyroid function, metabolism and brain development. The study highlights that teenage girls and women of childbearing age are particularly at risk, as they already have low iodine intake. While some manufacturers fortify their products, there is no formal requirement to do so, leading to concerns about public health outcomes as plant-based diets grow in popularity.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers suggest that requiring all non-dairy alternatives to be fortified with iodine could prevent average declines in nutrient intake. Dietitians recommend that consumers check labels for fortification and consider other dietary sources of iodine.
